stem.en: Looking back over the whole journey - membrane, wall, compartments, nucleus, division - what did every one of those innovations have in common?

text.en: Each solved a problem created by the success of the one before it.
Each was an improvement the cell worked out it needed in advance.

feedback.en: The trap the course has warned about from lesson one. Nothing here planned anything.
The last one makes cells smaller, deliberately.

text.en: Each appeared at the same time, as a complete package.

feedback.en: They arrived in order, and the order is the story.

explanation.en:
**Why "each solved a problem created by the one before" is right**

The membrane held the molecules together and cut them off from supplies. Selectivity fixed that and left the cell soft. A wall fixed that and let pressure build. Compartments handled a crowded interior and needed coordinating. A nucleus protected the instructions and made them awkward to read. Growth ran into a limit and division answered it.

That chain is the reason you can now explain why each part exists instead of listing what each part is called.

**Why the others are not**

- **Worked out in advance** - the one habit this course has argued against throughout.
- **Each made the cell larger** - division does the opposite, on purpose.
- **All at once** - the sequence is the whole point.

hints.en: Try listing what each innovation broke, not just what it fixed.
